Score changed from 0 (Unknown) to 4 (Yes) on the strength of KRA's official "File & Pay" and "Lipa Ushuru na M-Pesa" pages, which describe return filing on iTax, generation of a payment slip/e-slip, and direct payment via KRA Paybill 222222 (M-Pesa) or *222# — i.e. e-payment capability linked to an instant payment system. revised_comments: Kenya's Kenya Revenue Authority operates iTax (itax.kra.go.ke), an official online portal where individual and business taxpayers file income tax, VAT, PAYE and other returns. Taxpayers generate an e-slip/Payment Registration Number after filing and can pay directly via the "Lipa Ushuru na M-Pesa" service (KRA Paybill 222222, or by dialling *222#), which settles through Safaricom's M-Pesa mobile money platform, alongside standard bank RTGS/EFT channels. The portal therefore combines e-filing with direct e-payment capability linked to an instant/mobile payment system.

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: No strong evidence of formal pro-poor governance mechanisms (e.g., mandated consumer/low-income representation in scheme governance) for PesaLink; AfricaNenda's SIIPS case study notes PesaLink lacks a pro-poor mandate (bank-led scheme with minimal regulator input beyond oversight). Kenya's National Payments Strategy is explicitly oriented toward inclusion, but this is policy direction rather than a documented scheme-level pro-poor governance mechanism.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Both originally cited sources were fetched and support the score. AfricaNenda's SIIPS 2022 case study on PesaLink states explicitly that "there is no clear governance role for the Central Bank of Kenya beyond oversight of the scheme, and it lacks a pro-poor mandate" — PesaLink's decision-making body is the IPSL executive management, drawn from member banks, with no reserved seats or mandated input mechanism for consumer/vulnerable-group representatives. A further search found an October 2025 trade-press piece (Marketia) corroborating that this governance gap persists: PesaLink remains wholly owned by the Kenya Bankers Association, with an industry source quoted saying governance "should be representative of the payment participants... it's something we would definitely need to look into." Kenya's National Payments Strategy 2022-2025 sets an inclusion-oriented vision at the policy level but is not itself a scheme-level pro-poor governance mechanism. Score of 1 (No) is confirmed. Year corrected from blank to 2025 to reflect the most recent corroborating evidence.
revised_comments: Kenya's national instant payment scheme, PesaLink, is governed by Integrated Payment Services Limited (IPSL), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Kenya Bankers Association, whose decision-making body comprises representatives of member banks. There is no reserved seat, consumer advisory board, or formal mandate for input from small providers, consumer representatives, or vulnerable-population interests in the scheme's governance documents, and the Central Bank of Kenya's role is limited to regulatory oversight rather than governance participation. Kenya's National Payments Strategy 2022-2025 articulates an inclusion-oriented vision for the payments ecosystem at the policy level, but this sits outside PesaLink's own governance structure. Industry commentary as recently as late 2025 continues to identify the lack of representative, inclusive governance as an unresolved gap for the scheme.

revised_comments: According to the World Bank's Global Findex Database 2025 (survey fieldwork conducted in 2024), 90.7% of Kenyan adults reported having made or received a digital payment (via mobile money, a bank-linked card or phone, or online) in the reference period, one of the highest rates globally and reflecting the deep penetration of M-Pesa and related mobile money services. The figure captures broad digital payment activity rather than narrowly defined 'instant payment system' transactions in the past 90 days, but indicates very high active usage of digital payment channels among the adult population.

Score changed from 0 (Unknown) to 2 (Partial) based on: Safaricom's IVR-based M-Pesa balance-reading service for visually impaired customers (launched 2021) and Dot Braille Watch partnership; the Kenya Bankers' Association's 2019 disability-inclusion roadmap for banks (staff training, accessible branches, accessible mobile/online banking); and peer-reviewed evidence (PLOS One, 2025) and a Sightsavers-commissioned landscape study (2023), both finding that some accommodations exist (voice-enabled apps, screen readers, agent assistance) but that provision is inconsistent, mostly informal or ad hoc, not backed by enforced accessibility standards, and gaps remain (inaccessible USSD codes, non-functional screen readers, ATM height/braille issues). This is 'Partial' rather than 'Yes' (comprehensive, standards-based accessibility) or 'No' (nothing exists).
revised_comments: Kenya's digital payment ecosystem shows partial accommodation of persons with disabilities. Safaricom's M-Pesa offers an IVR-based balance-checking service (dial 234) for visually impaired customers and has partnered on a Dot Braille Watch enabling braille reading of M-Pesa SMS notifications. The Kenya Bankers Association adopted disability inclusion as a strategic goal in 2019 and has since promoted staff training, priority queuing, and accessible mobile/online banking features among member banks. However, independent research (a 2025 peer-reviewed study and a 2023 Sightsavers-commissioned landscape assessment) finds these accommodations are inconsistently implemented: USSD codes remain difficult for visually impaired users, screen-reader functionality is sometimes non-functional, and physical barriers (ATM height, lack of braille or audio) persist, with most institutions still designing services for the general population rather than to a documented accessibility standard.

Definition: Percentage of government payments (G2P disbursements including salaries, pensions, social transfers) made through instant digital payment system rather than cash or check, reflecting government adoption and modernization.
Comments: No quantified estimate of the share of government payments digitized (0–5 scale thresholds) was collected in this run. Evidence found shows active digitization (e.g., Inua Jamii via eCitizen/M-Pesa), but not a national % across government payments.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A single fast-check search surfaced a clearly authoritative primary source (Kenya's National Treasury) plus corroborating World Bank project documentation, so this row was moved from the fast path to full verification rather than confirmed as Unknown. No single official statistic gives an aggregate percentage of all G2P disbursements made digitally, so the score is a composite judgement across major G2P categories rather than a single reported figure: (i) civil service salaries have been paid via the electronic IPPD payroll system since 1998; (ii) public service pensions moved to a fully digital, ERP-based payment system from July 2025 (Business Daily, August 2025), replacing a previously manual/delay-prone process; (iii) the flagship Inua Jamii/NSNP cash transfer programmes (Older Persons, OVC, PWSD, HSNP) pay virtually all beneficiaries electronically via contracted bank/PSP accounts, with a recent World Bank Implementation Completion Report noting the Hunger Safety Net Programme achieved '100 percent coverage through the new electronic payment system.' Given salaries and social cash transfers are effectively fully digitised and pensions only reached full digitisation in mid-2025 (a recent transition, with historical backlogs/manual processing), a rating of 4 (70-89%) is used rather than 5, allowing for transitional/residual manual processing and the absence of one single consolidated national percentage. This is a reasoned composite estimate rather than a directly reported percentage; flagged for human review to confirm whether a more precise official aggregate figure exists that might justify 5.
revised_comments: The Government of Kenya has pursued near-universal digitisation of government-to-person payments since a November 2013 presidential directive mandating that all government payments be made digitally. Civil service salaries have been paid through the electronic Integrated Personnel Payroll Database (IPPD) since 1998, and from August 2025 the National Treasury extended the same integrated payments system to public service pensions, replacing a previously manual, delay-prone and fraud-exposed process. The flagship National Safety Net Programme (Inua Jamii, covering older persons, orphans and vulnerable children, and persons with severe disabilities) pays beneficiaries electronically through six contracted bank/payment service providers, and the related Hunger Safety Net Programme has achieved full coverage through its new electronic payment system. Taken together, the large majority of government payments to citizens, spanning salaries, pensions and major social transfer programmes, are now made digitally, though a single official aggregate percentage across all G2P payment types is not published.

revision_notes: A single fast-check search surfaced clearly authoritative sources (a GSMA Mobile for Humanitarian Innovation report and an FSD Kenya landscape assessment), so this row was moved from the fast path to full verification rather than confirmed as Unknown. Score changed from 0 (Unknown) to 2 (Partial) on the basis that Kenya enacted Legal Notice No. 90 (30 May 2025) under the Kenya Information and Communications Act, formally recognising Refugee ID Cards as valid documentation for SIM card registration for the first time, opening a legal pathway to mobile money access (GSMA, 2026). However, FSD Kenya's 2026 landscape assessment finds practical access remains partial: an estimated 30% of the roughly 836,000 registered refugees and asylum seekers hold both an ID and a mobile money account, fewer than 10% are formally banked, and implementation gaps persist (documentation delays, inconsistent KYC application, uncollected Refugee IDs). Full, formal bank-account access is not yet in place. This is 'Partial' rather than 'Yes' (full legal and practical access) or 'No' (no access at all).
revised_comments: Refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya gained a significant legal pathway to digital payment access on 30 May 2025, when the government enacted Legal Notice No. 90 under the Kenya Information and Communications Act, formally recognising Refugee ID Cards for SIM card registration and, by extension, mobile money service access (previously mobile accounts were largely accessed informally via Kenyan proxies). Mobile money, primarily M-Pesa, is the dominant financial channel for refugees, underpinning daily transactions, remittances and humanitarian cash transfers. In practice, however, access remains partial: roughly 30% of Kenya's approximately 836,000 registered refugees and asylum seekers hold both a Refugee ID and a mobile money account, fewer than 10% are formally banked, and barriers persist around documentation delays, inconsistent application of KYC requirements, and limited interoperability between refugee identity systems and national ID/KYC infrastructure. Formal bank-account access for refugees, distinct from mobile money, remains largely unavailable outside partner-led programmes.
